title: Κυνόδηκτος
titleEn: The Man Bitten by a Dog
part: The Man Bitten by a Dog (Chambry 177 · Perry 64)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 177 (= Perry 64). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Δηχθείς τις ὑπὸ κυνὸς περιῄει ζητῶν τὸν ἰασόμενον.
sentences.tr: Dēchtheis tis hypo kynos periēiei zētōn ton iasomenon.
sentences.l: A man, having been bitten by a dog, was going about seeking the one who would cure him.
sentences.n: τὸν ἰασόμενον is a future participle with the article — Greek's regular way of naming a person by the office he is to perform, "the man who is to cure". περιῄει is the imperfect of περίειμι, the round of calls he made.

sentences.t: Εἰπόντος δέ τινος οὕτως ὡς ἄρα δέοι αὐτὸν ἄρτῳ τὸ αἷμα ἐκμάξαντα τῷ δακόντι κυνὶ βαλεῖν, ὑποτυχὼν ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἐὰν τοῦτο πράξω, δεήσει με ὑπὸ πάντων τῶν ἐν τῇ πόλει κυνῶν δάκνεσθαι. »
sentences.tr: Eipontos de tinos houtōs hōs ara deoi auton artōi to haima ekmaxanta tōi dakonti kyni balein, hypotychōn ephē· « All’ ean touto praxō, deēsei me hypo pantōn tōn en tēi polei kynōn daknesthai. »
sentences.l: But someone having spoken thus, that he must wipe the blood off with a loaf and throw it to the dog that had bitten him, taking-up-the-word he said: « But if I do this, it will be necessary for me to be bitten by all the dogs in the city. »
sentences.i: And when someone told him he ought to wipe the blood off with a loaf and throw it to the dog that had bitten him, he took up the word and said: « But if I do that, I shall have to be bitten by every dog in the city. »
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute, εἰπόντος τινός. ὡς with the optative δέοι is indirect speech after a verb of saying, the optative marking the words as reported rather than the narrator's own. ὑποτυχών is "taking up the word", to reply — nothing physical is seized. The cure offered is folk medicine: blood sopped from the wound in bread and given back to the dog that drew it.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ ἡ τῶν ἀνθρώπων πονηρία δελεαζομένη ἔτι μᾶλλον ἀδικεῖν παροξύνεται.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai hē tōn anthrōpōn ponēria deleazomenē eti mallon adikein paroxynetai.
sentences.l: So too the wickedness of men, being baited, is goaded on to do wrong still more.
sentences.n: δελεάζω is to put down bait for a creature, and the metaphor stays half-open here, since the loaf really would have been bait. παροξύνω is to sharpen on a whetstone, hence to goad. ἀδικεῖν is an infinitive of the end the goading drives toward.
